options.A: Cannot be determined
options.B: K

38.stem: In a survey of 250 people, 150 own a car and 100 do not. Of the car owners, 36 also own a bicycle; of those who do not own a car, 54 own a bicycle. If one bicycle owner is selected at random, what is the probability that the person owns a car?

39.stem: At a company, 60% of employees work in the engineering division. Of the engineering employees, 40% work remotely. Of all non-engineering employees, 30% work remotely. If 180 employees work remotely, how many employees does the company have in total?

40.stem: At a company, 30% of all employees work in the sales division. Of the employees in the sales division, 25% exceeded their quota this quarter. If 18 sales-division employees exceeded their quota, how many employees does the company have in total?

42.stem: How many more units did Z sell than W?

43.stem: A study of 300 patients tracked whether they received a new treatment and whether they recovered within a week. 180 patients received the treatment, and 75% of them recovered. Of the patients who did NOT receive the treatment, 40% recovered. What percent of ALL recovered patients had received the treatment? Round to the nearest whole percent.

44.stem: A cyclist rides 30 kilometers at a speed of 20 kilometers per hour and then rides another 30 kilometers at a speed of 30 kilometers per hour. What is the cyclist's average speed for the entire 60-kilometer trip, in kilometers per hour, rounded to the nearest tenth?

options.A: 5% decrease
options.B: 5% increase
options.C: 0% (no change)
options.D: 45% increase

49.stem: Which choice best states the main inference that the passage supports?

options.A: Languages that spread through conquest and trade are more sophisticated, having shed the irregularities adult learners find arbitrary
options.B: Children master irregular systems of agreement and evidentiality less readily than adult learners do
options.C: A language's grammatical complexity reflects the circumstances of its transmission more than the abilities of its speakers
options.D: Languages spoken by small, isolated communities are grammatically simpler because limited contact pares their grammars down

50.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "address" most nearly mean?

options.A: skill in handling situations
options.B: the act of directing a letter
options.C: a formal speech to an audience
options.D: the location of a residence

51.stem: The passage is primarily structured to

options.A: argue that Tocqueville ultimately rejected democracy in favor of aristocratic government.
options.B: trace the influence of Democracy in America on later democratic theory.
options.C: acknowledge a familiar reading of Tocqueville before showing how it omits the qualification that reverses its meaning.
options.D: contrast the violent despotism of earlier eras with the peaceful stability that mature democracies achieve.

52.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?

options.A: Early printers competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions of the classical authors.
options.B: Across Europe the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over within a few decades of the first printed editions.
options.C: In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.
options.D: Literacy rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared, well before any schooling campaigns began.

53.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author attributes the emergence of chemistry chiefly to a change in

options.A: the growing social prestige of practitioners such as Newton and Boyle, who lent the new science their names.
options.B: how experimental results were shared, rather than in whether experiments were performed.
options.C: the discovery that careful experiment was superior to the mystical speculation alchemists had favored.
options.D: the abandonment of the distillation and assaying techniques inherited from alchemical workshops.

54.stem: The authors of Text 2 would most likely characterize the conclusion drawn in Text 1 as

options.A: correct without qualification, because a witness's certainty carries no information about accuracy at any stage of an investigation or trial
options.B: mistaken, because confident eyewitnesses turn out to be almost always accurate, whenever in the process their confidence happens to be recorded
options.C: correct in general but based on confidence measurements taken after the identification had already been distorted.
options.D: unsupported, because the laboratory studies behind the earlier consensus cannot tell us how memory behaves in real investigations and courtrooms

55.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence "The disproportion is deliberate; the failure is the education the successes merely displayed" in the text?

options.A: It explains why the author devoted so much space to a brief, unsuccessful episode.
options.B: It introduces a new failure that the rest of the memoir will examine.
options.C: It criticizes readers who value diplomatic successes over failures.
options.D: It concedes that the negotiation was less important than the author first suggested.

56.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen Marchetti's argument?

options.A: Beaver colonies have multiplied along several Yellowstone streams in the years since the wolves were returned to the park.
options.B: Wolves reintroduced to other national parks have cut local deer numbers within a few seasons.
options.C: In valleys where wolves are abundant but groundwater is deep, willow cover has continued to decline.
options.D: Elk numbers fell sharply in the years just after the wolves returned to the park.

57.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen Vogel's argument?

options.A: Towns that gained a new local paper saw local advertising revenue rise sharply within two years
options.B: After their local papers closed, residents scored markedly lower on tests of local political knowledge
options.C: In towns that lost their local papers, civic participation declined even among residents who had never subscribed
options.D: Residents who relied on national outlets knew far more about federal policy than about the affairs of their own towns

58.stem: What is the main rhetorical effect of the final sentence?

options.A: It suggests that orchards and hedgerows never belonged in a forest count in the first place.
options.B: It urges surveyors to drop the continuous-canopy rule and restore the earlier count of orchards, hedgerows, and woodlots.
options.C: It confirms the environmental groups' reading of the shrinking figure as evidence of accelerating loss.
options.D: It locates the apparent decline in the changed method of measurement rather than in any actual loss of trees.

59.stem: Which choice is most strongly supported by the text?

options.A: Theories that forbid very little are the most scientifically valuable.
options.B: Auxiliary assumptions about instruments are always the component that turns out to be false.
options.C: Because an anomaly implicates a whole bundle of assumptions, it need not require rejecting the central theory it appears to contradict.
options.D: A scientific theory should be discarded as soon as a single observation contradicts it.

60.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.A: It traces the gradual technical improvement of the printing press over several decades.
options.B: It argues that the printing press had no meaningful effect on European thought.
options.C: It contrasts the reading habits of scribes with those of early commercial printers.
options.D: It presents a common explanation and then complicates it by locating the decisive cause elsewhere.

73.stem: The final sentence ('A cascade, it turns out, requires a slope') most directly implies that

options.A: restoring the park's willow populations was the primary goal of reintroducing wolves to Yellowstone.
options.B: climate swings and a rising bison population proved more powerful ecological forces than wolf predation.
options.C: the wolves' impact depended on environmental conditions already conducive to change.
options.D: predators exert no measurable influence on the ecosystems into which they are reintroduced.

74.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.A: Runners carrying knotted cords kept the state's records of tribute and storehouse inventory.
options.B: The road network existed primarily to move armies quickly between the empire's distant provinces.
options.C: The Inca roads are better understood as infrastructure for centralized economic management than as a military system.
options.D: The empire spanned regions of sharply different climates, and its storehouses held textiles, grain, and dried potatoes alike.

75.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the historian's argument?

options.A: The kingdom's total coin production remained constant throughout the period.
options.B: The expansion in minting coincided exactly with the start of a major war.
options.C: Coins from the period are concentrated in caches near fortified military camps.
options.D: Coins from the expansion period are found distributed widely across market towns far from any garrison.

76.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the researcher's claim?

options.A: The classes of 22 and 30 students had equal average scores, indicating that class size did not affect reading performance.
options.B: The class of 38 students scored 66 on average, the lowest of the four averages the researcher recorded.
options.C: The largest class, of 38 students, scored highest on the reading test, outperforming even the smallest class, which had only 15.
options.D: The smallest class, of 15 students, had the highest average score at 88, while the largest, of 38, had the lowest at 66.

77.stem: Which choice best describes the point the philosopher draws from her two examples?

options.A: The single term memory conceals distinct faculties that can operate and fail separately.
options.B: Memory functions as a single unified capacity despite its varied contents.
options.C: People tend to forget their childhood addresses before forgetting their childhood homes.
options.D: Recalling images is generally more reliable than recalling factual information.

78.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.A: Because volcanic ash weathers so slowly, the minerals it releases come too late to be of any use to the crops of a single generation.
options.B: The agricultural richness produced by volcanic ash draws people to settle in hazardous places.
options.C: Volcanic eruptions occur more often near densely populated regions than in areas where few people have settled.
options.D: People go on settling on the flanks of active volcanoes chiefly because they underestimate how often eruptions destroy the fields below.

79.stem: Which choice best describes the cartographer's dilemma?

options.A: The fishermen had begun demanding a more detailed and jagged version of the map.
options.B: A more accurate map risked discarding the familiar shapes that had become practical navigational tools.
options.C: Her earlier map had been intentionally falsified to mislead rival cartographers.
options.D: The new instruments were too imprecise to justify redrawing the coastline at all.

80.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the researcher's claim?

options.A: City D, with the most charging stations at 18 per 10,000 people, had the highest electric-vehicle share at 22%.
options.B: City A had an electric-vehicle share of 4%, the lowest of the four cities compared.
options.C: City B and City C reported identical electric-vehicle shares despite having different numbers of charging stations.
options.D: City D had the fewest charging stations of the four cities yet the highest electric-vehicle share, at 22%.

81.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.A: Coffeehouses replaced taverns as the main gathering places of seventeenth-century England once patrons found that drink dulled their debate.
options.B: Merchants, poets, and natural philosophers rarely reached agreement in the coffeehouse arguments that ranged from shipping rates to Newton's optics.
options.C: Coffeehouses earned the nickname "penny universities" because a patron could linger among them for hours for the price of a single cup.
options.D: Coffeehouses spread news and ideas so effectively that some historians compare their impact to that of formal education.

82.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

options.A: It sets two competing accounts of color perception against each other and finally endorses neither of them.
options.B: It defends the traditional claim that vocabulary shapes perception against recent experimental challenges.
options.C: It presents a popular claim about language and color and then marshals experimental evidence that refutes it entirely.
options.D: It introduces a strong version of a hypothesis and then replaces it with a weaker version the evidence supports.

83.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?

options.A: Of the 100 students who received the tutoring, 16 failed the exam and the other 84 passed it.
options.B: The same number of students passed the exam in the tutored group as in the group that received no tutoring.
options.C: More of the 100 tutored students failed the exam than of the 100 students who were not tutored.
options.D: Among the 100 tutored students, 84 passed, compared with 55 of the 100 who were not tutored.

84.stem: How does Text 2's characterization of the "invaders" most directly complicate the account in Text 1?

options.A: By arguing that the late empire's tax base was far sounder than the traditional account allows.
options.B: By suggesting that many of those Text 1 treats as external destroyers were already integrated into the imperial system.
options.C: By denying that Germanic peoples played any part in the collapse of the western empire.
options.D: By claiming that the empire's collapse arrived suddenly with the sack of the capital rather than through decades of decay.

85.stem: The student wants to emphasize that independent lines of evidence converge on the same estimate for dark matter. Which choice most effectively uses the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Ordinary matter, the kind that makes up stars and planets, accounts for about 5% of the universe's mass-energy.
options.B: Data from the cosmic microwave background — the faint radiation left over from the early universe — put dark matter at about 27% of the universe's total mass-energy.
options.C: Three independent methods (galaxy-rotation measurements, CMB data, and gravitational lensing) all put dark matter at roughly 26-27% of the universe's mass-energy.
options.D: Dark energy accounts for about 68% of the universe's mass-energy, far more than dark matter contributes.

86.stem: The student wants to highlight a practical use that the pollen finding makes possible. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Because trace lead levels in the honey from all 50 rooftop hives were well below safety limits, city beekeepers can market it as safe to eat without further testing.
options.B: City honey already sells at premium prices at local markets, where buyers are willing to pay more for a product harvested from hives in the city.
options.C: Chemists who analyzed honey from 50 city rooftop hives found that the pollen it contained matched the ornamental-garden and street-tree species nearby.
options.D: Because each neighborhood's plants leave a distinct pollen fingerprint, the honey can be traced back to the specific area where it was produced.

87.stem: The student wants to emphasize that a single factor was behind several of the observed changes. Which choice most effectively uses the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Fishers reported changes in the species they caught after warming waters shifted fish ranges northward during 2016.
options.B: Coral bleaching in 2016 reduced revenue from tourism, and in that same year fishers along the coast reported changes in the species they caught.
options.C: Rising ocean temperatures drove several changes at once—bleaching corals, shifting fish ranges northward, and intensifying tropical storms.
options.D: Tropical storms grew more intense in 2016, the same year in which coral bleaching sharply reduced the revenue that the region earned from tourism.

88.stem: The student wants to generalize the finding in a way a skeptical reader—wary of sweeping claims—would accept. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Because the only sample without self-healing growth came from a freshwater river site, seawater must be what triggers the effect in every structure the Romans ever built.
options.B: In 9 of the 10 marine structures sampled, the concrete showed self-healing mineral growth, indicating the effect is characteristic of Roman seawater concrete.
options.C: Unlike Roman concrete, which was mixed with volcanic ash, modern Portland cement contains none and shows no comparable mineral growth sealing the cracks that open in it.
options.D: The self-healing mineral aluminous tobermorite forms when seawater reacts with the volcanic ash in the concrete, filling cracks in the harbor structures as they open.

89.stem: The student wants to note a limitation a cautious reader should keep in mind. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: The colonies exposed to the pesticide were compared against a group of unexposed control colonies.
options.B: The study's reach was narrow: it lasted a single season, covered only one region of France, and tested only honeybees.
options.C: The exposure levels used in the study matched the concentrations that bees actually encounter in real agricultural fields.
options.D: Colonies exposed to the pesticide lost 30% more workers over the foraging season than the unexposed control colonies did over the same period.

90.stem: The student wants to point out an exception to the general migratory pattern. Which choice most effectively uses the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: The warbler species that did migrate departed in flocks rather than singly, a habit the study recorded throughout the whole of the autumn season.
options.B: Although most of the studied warblers migrated south by October, the yellow-rumped warbler remained in the north through the winter.
options.C: The blackpoll warbler flew a nonstop three-day route across the Atlantic, an unusually demanding crossing for a bird weighing barely twelve grams.
options.D: Most of the twelve warbler species in the study had migrated south by October, departing in flocks once the northern nights turned cold.

91.stem: The student wants to emphasize the causal chain linking the wolves to the recovery of the riverside trees. Which choice most effectively uses the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995.
options.B: Beaver colonies increased from one to twelve after the reintroduction.
options.C: Songbird numbers rose following the wolves' return.
options.D: After wolves returned in 1995, elk avoided the open valleys, allowing the willow and aspen along the rivers to regrow.

92.stem: The student wants to show how several findings together support a single conclusion about exercise and memory. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?

options.A: One study found that aerobic exercise increases the size of the hippocampus, which is the brain region most closely tied to the forming and retrieving of memories.
options.B: Exercise enlarges the hippocampus and raises BDNF (a neuron-supporting protein), changes that help explain why regular exercisers score better on memory tests.
options.C: Exercise also tends to improve mood — an effect that appears across every age group alongside the measured increases in hippocampal size and in levels of the protein BDNF.
options.D: The effects of exercise appear consistently across all age groups, in studies measuring hippocampal size, levels of the protein BDNF, and performance on memory tests.

93.stem: The student wants to emphasize the sequence of warning signs that preceded the eruption. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?

options.A: In the weeks before the March 12 eruption, the warning signs mounted in order: first earthquakes, then ground bulging, then a spike in sulfur gas.
options.B: Scientists now use signals like these as eruption warnings, which is why monitoring instruments are installed on volcanoes that have been quiet for decades.
options.C: The volcano erupted on March 12, and the eruption is now among the most closely documented events of its kind anywhere in the region's recent history.
options.D: Sulfur gas emissions spiked in the hours before the eruption, rising far above the levels the monitoring station had recorded in any earlier month of that year.

94.stem: The writer wants to explain why the researchers conducted the second experiment. Which choice most effectively uses the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Plants in the second experiment, which ran the same apparatus on normal air at the identical temperature, showed no extra growth at all over the whole trial.
options.B: They conducted the second experiment to rule out the possibility that heat from the apparatus, rather than the CO2, was causing the extra growth.
options.C: In the first experiment, plants supplied with extra CO2 grew 30% taller than they otherwise would have, a difference large enough to demand an explanation.
options.D: Taken together, the two experiments confirmed that it was the CO2 and not the temperature of the apparatus that was responsible for the extra growth.

95.stem: The student wants to introduce the role of chlorophyll to an audience unfamiliar with photosynthesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

options.A: Chlorophyll, a green pigment in plant leaves, absorbs the light energy that plants use to make food.
options.B: The energy that chlorophyll absorbs is used to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugar.
options.C: Oxygen is released as a byproduct when carbon dioxide and water are converted into sugar.
options.D: Chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly at red and blue wavelengths, reflecting the green that remains.

96.stem: The student wants to emphasize the counterintuitive nature of the finding that cleaner air sped up warming. Which choice most effectively accomplishes this goal?

options.A: Before the regulations took effect, cleaner air over the oceans had been expected to slow the overall pace of global warming.
options.B: Surprisingly, cutting sulfur pollution stripped away a layer of sunlight-reflecting particles, and some ocean regions ended up warming faster as a result.
options.C: The sulfur particles released in ship exhaust had been reflecting sunlight back toward space and brightening the layers of cloud that form above the ocean.
options.D: New regulations that took effect in 2020 sharply cut the sulfur pollution released by ship exhaust over the world's oceans, where large vessels burn heavy fuel.
